question: How stable are relative pairwise representational similarities among a broad zoo of pretrained vision models when the evaluation stimuli change, which model and dataset attributes are associated with that stability, and when does representational similarity track downstream performance differences?

key_findings.claim: The paper contributes a useful cross-dataset consistency statistic, but it measures affine-invariant agreement of relative model-pair similarities rather than transfer of absolute representational similarity values.
key_findings.evidence: For each evaluation dataset, the authors vectorize CKA values over the same model pairs and define consistency between two datasets as the Pearson correlation of those vectors. This directly answers whether model-pair similarities preserve a linear ordering across stimulus sets. Pearson correlation is unchanged by an affine rescaling or shift of either vector, so a correlation near one can coexist with materially different absolute CKA levels. The method section states this relative interpretation clearly, but later language about whether similarities themselves transfer can be read more broadly than the statistic warrants.

key_findings.claim: Across all 64 models and 23 datasets, relative model-pair ordering is broadly stable rather than generally non-transferable.
key_findings.evidence: The mean Pearson correlation over all dataset pairs is 0.756 with standard deviation 0.124. The authors correctly interpret this in Section 4.4 as substantial transferability in the ordering of pairwise similarities, alongside meaningful heterogeneity across model groups and dataset pairs. This numerical result is important context for the paper's stronger discussion framing that pairwise similarities are dataset-dependent: the main aggregate effect is high relative stability with identifiable exceptions, not wholesale instability.

key_findings.claim: The central descriptive result is a separation between high absolute similarity and high cross-dataset consistency: image-text models are most mutually similar, while self-supervised model relationships are most stable across stimuli.
key_findings.evidence: Image-text models form a cluster of high CKA values, yet self-supervised models have the highest distributions of cross-dataset correlations; supervised pairs are least consistent under the primary linear-CKA analysis. This distinction is scientifically useful because it prevents high representational alignment on one dataset from being conflated with dataset-invariant alignment. Dataset heatmaps further show that aircraft and medical datasets are frequent low-consistency outliers and that within-category dataset pairs tend to be more consistent.

key_findings.claim: The title-level causal implication that objective drives consistency is not identified by the main observational model-zoo comparison.
key_findings.evidence: The 64 checkpoints are not assigned factorially: objective, training data, model family, parameter count, lineage, and extraction layer are strongly correlated. The paper explicitly notes, for example, that only image-text models occupy the XLarge data category, all ImageNet-21k models are supervised, and no image-text model is trained on ImageNet-1k or ImageNet-21k. Representations are also extracted systematically differently by objective: supervised penultimate layers, SSL average-pooling or final-normalized layers, and image-text image encoders. Boxplots stratified one attribute at a time therefore show association, not an isolated objective effect.

key_findings.claim: The statistical summaries treat heavily dependent dyads and dataset pairs as if their empirical distributions were direct evidence about factor importance, without hierarchical uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Each of the 2,016 all-model dyads shares its constituent checkpoints with many other dyads, many checkpoints are near-duplicate family members or scales, and every one of the 253 dataset pairs shares each dataset with 22 other pairs. Category panels also have unequal numbers of models and therefore unequal vector lengths and precision. The paper reports box distributions, means, standard deviations, and qualitative ordering but no model-family cluster bootstrap, dyadic mixed-effects model, dataset-level block bootstrap, permutation null preserving dependence, confidence interval for median differences, or multiplicity-adjusted category contrast. Quadratic enumeration can consequently over-weight densely sampled model lineages and make visual differences appear more certain than the effective number of independent models or datasets supports.

key_findings.claim: Metric robustness is real at the level of the broad objective trend but does not establish metric-independent ordering of all scientific conclusions.
key_findings.evidence: Linear CKA, local RBF CKA, and RSA Spearman all retain objective as an important grouping, which is a useful robustness result. However, the paper reports only moderate agreement between some global/local consistency values, and exact rankings change: under local RBF CKA, supervised pairs become more consistent than image-text pairs, and ImageNet-21k pairs outrank ImageNet-1k pairs, reversing the global linear-CKA ordering. Moreover, later theory shows mean-centered RSA and CKA are closely related, so agreement between these measures is not three fully independent replications of the construct.

key_findings.claim: The sampling audit supports the practicality of global CKA at 10,000 ImageNet examples, while simultaneously showing that local similarity is substantially more stimulus-sensitive.
key_findings.evidence: On ImageNet-1k subsets, most CKA variants stabilize around 10,000 samples, whereas RBF CKA with sigma 0.2 requires 30,000. Across 500 independently sampled subsets for six anchor models, linear CKA is visually stable and the local RBF estimator retains greater variability even at 30,000 images. This is a strong computational sanity check for the primary metric, although it is performed on one broad dataset and six anchors rather than across all 23 dataset distributions and all 64 models.

anchors.section: Appendix C, bootstrap interpretation and subsampling rule

key_findings.claim: The reported relationship between representation and behavior is dataset-conditioned and correlational, not a validated model-selection or causal prediction rule.
key_findings.evidence: For each dataset, the authors correlate pairwise linear CKA with absolute gaps between three-seed linear-probe accuracies. Negative correlations are strongest for many natural single-domain and structured datasets, weak for ImageNet-1k and other multi-domain datasets, and low for specialized datasets; category distributions overlap and SVHN is an explicit single-domain outlier. No held-out test asks whether CKA measured on one dataset prospectively predicts a performance gap on another, improves model selection over metadata or performance baselines, or causally constrains task strategy. Both CKA and probe accuracy are themselves functions of the evaluation dataset.

anchors.section: Appendix J, category overlap and unquantified context hypothesis

key_findings.claim: The appendix's best controlled intervention shows that training-data domain can materially change consistency, directly narrowing the main claim that training data is comparatively unimportant.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix I compares AlexNet, DenseNet161, ResNet18, and ResNet50 trained with the same supervised objective on either ImageNet-1k or Places365, holding architecture type and size class relatively fixed. Places365-trained pairs have higher consistency than ImageNet-trained pairs, and the authors conclude that training-data domain significantly influences consistency. The main text's weaker training-data result concerns mostly coarse data-size categories among broad general-purpose models and is confounded with objective; it should not be generalized to training data as a whole.

anchors.section: Appendix I, controlled ImageNet versus Places365 design

key_findings.claim: The six-anchor analysis reduces architecture and size confounding but cannot by itself isolate objective and should not be described as a controlled objective experiment.
key_findings.evidence: The anchors match two broad architecture/scale templates across objective groups: OpenCLIP RN50 and ViT-L, SimCLR RN50 and DINOv2 ViT-L, and supervised ResNet50 and ViT-L. Yet these checkpoints differ in training corpus, algorithm family, augmentations, pretraining duration, and exact parameterization, and DINOv2 versus SimCLR also spans a large data and method difference. The analysis shows the main descriptive pattern is not confined to broad architecture or size, but it does not provide same-data, same-architecture, same-optimizer retraining with only the objective changed.

Appendix Table 2, checkpoint provenance and extraction layers

key_findings.claim: The artifact makes the study unusually inspectable, but its documented main reproduction path does not regenerate the paper's chosen local-similarity setting.
key_findings.evidence: The public repository exposes model and dataset configurations, feature extraction, unbiased CKA computation, upper-triangle dyad extraction, aggregation notebooks, linear probing, and downloadable intermediate results. Inspection at commit 99d8051f9985f86d1bc64fd43243d30b408c2606 confirms that the default CKA implementation is unbiased and the correlation notebooks use unique upper-triangle pairs. However, the README-recommended distance script hard-codes similarity_metric_config_local_global.json, whose RBF entry is sigma 0.4 on 10k-subset inputs, while Appendix F selects sigma 0.2 as the local metric and Appendix C requires 30k samples for it. The all-metric config contains sigma 0.2, but the documented command does not use it. The environment is only partially pinned, the pipeline assumes SLURM, and the figure-producing analysis remains notebook-centric without end-to-end regression assertions.

method.core_idea: Treat the evaluation dataset as an explicit axis of representational comparison: compute a vector of pairwise model similarities on each dataset, correlate the same vector across dataset pairs, and study how the resulting consistency distribution changes with model objectives, architectures, training data, size, dataset category, similarity metric, and downstream behavior.
method.mechanism: The study extracts L2-normalized final or penultimate representations from 64 pretrained vision checkpoints on the training split of 23 datasets. It computes unbiased CKA for every distinct model pair, primarily with a linear kernel on up to 10,000 stratified examples. For two datasets A and B and fixed model sets, Pearson correlation between their vectors of model-pair CKA values is the consistency statistic. Distributions of this statistic across dataset pairs are stratified by checkpoint metadata. RBF CKA and RSA provide local/global sensitivity analyses, six anchor checkpoints reduce architecture/size variation, linear-probe accuracy gaps supply a functional comparison, and an eight-model ImageNet-versus-Places extension probes training-domain effects.
assumptions: Pearson correlation between dyadic CKA vectors captures the scientifically relevant notion of transfer even though it discards absolute shifts and nonlinear reordering.
The selected 64-model zoo is representative enough that its attribute-conditioned distributions generalize beyond the sampled public checkpoints.
Objective labels summarize the operative training pressure despite large within-label variation among SSL and image-text methods.

Objective, architecture, training corpus, scale, family, pretraining duration, augmentation, and extraction layer can be interpreted separately from one-attribute-at-a-time observational stratification.
The objective-specific extraction conventions compare homologous semantic stages across supervised, SSL, and image-text systems.
All model-pair observations and all dataset-pair observations can be summarized empirically without accounting for their shared-node dependence.
Dense checkpoint families should receive weight proportional to their number of pairwise combinations rather than one weight per independent training lineage.
Model-group comparisons remain comparable despite 14 image-text, 20 SSL, and 30 supervised checkpoints yielding different dyad counts and estimator precision.
Images resized to 256 and center-cropped to 224 provide an equally appropriate stimulus transformation for models trained with different native resolutions and preprocessing recipes.
L2-normalizing every representation preserves the model information relevant to the intended similarity construct.
Linear CKA on 10,000 stratified examples is sufficiently stable outside ImageNet and across model pairs not included in the six-anchor bootstrap.
RBF bandwidth 0.2 has a comparable local meaning across representation dimensionalities after per-vector normalization.
Agreement of linear CKA, RBF CKA, and RSA is evidence of construct robustness even though these measures share mathematical structure and inputs.
Absolute linear-probe accuracy gap is an adequate proxy for functional difference and its correlation with CKA is not dominated by ceiling, class count, or difficulty effects.
Higher consistency implies a more stimulus-invariant relationship rather than a shared shortcut, shared preprocessing response, or restricted solution space.
Final-layer geometric alignment can bear on claims about a shared representation of reality without causal or cross-decoding validation of the represented content.

techniques.role: Defines similarity consistency as Pearson correlation between the same model-pair CKA vector on two datasets.
Measures global representational geometry between different-dimensional model features with finite-sample bias correction.
Contrasts local and increasingly global representation structure at sigma values from 0.2 through 0.8.
Supplies an alternative global representational-similarity analysis.
Groups checkpoint dyads by objective, architecture, data-size category, and parameter-size category.
Maps consistency across natural multi-domain, natural single-domain, specialized, and structured dataset pairs.
Caps linear-CKA computations at 10,000 examples and local RBF CKA at 30,000 after an ImageNet sensitivity study.
Uses 500 sampled ImageNet subsets to assess stimulus-sampling variability for representative model pairs.
Compares six matched broad architecture/size anchors against objective groups to reduce two metadata confounds.
Relates representational similarity to absolute top-1 accuracy differences after three-seed linear probing.
Compares four CNN architectures pretrained on ImageNet-1k versus Places365 under a shared supervised objective.
Exposes extraction, similarity, probing, aggregation, and figure workflows plus downloadable intermediate outputs.

evaluations.setting: 64 pretrained vision checkpoints spanning 14 image-text, 20 self-supervised, and 30 supervised models on 23 vision datasets
evaluations.metric: Pearson correlation between all-model linear-CKA dyad vectors for every dataset pair
evaluations.result: Mean cross-dataset consistency is 0.756 with standard deviation 0.124, indicating broadly preserved relative model similarity with substantial dataset-pair variation
evaluations.baseline: Descriptive all-model distribution; no shuffled-dyad, family-balanced, or hierarchical uncertainty baseline

evaluations.result: SSL-containing pairs have the highest consistency distributions, supervised pairs the weakest under linear CKA; architecture and size panels show smaller separations

evaluations.result: Within-category dataset pairs are often more consistent; FGVC Aircraft, diabetic retinopathy, and PCAM are prominent low-consistency cases, with different structure for SSL versus image-text/supervised comparisons
evaluations.baseline: Manual dataset taxonomy; no measured domain-distance, background-context, or compositional-statistics baseline

evaluations.metric: Cross-metric correlations and category-conditioned consistency distributions
evaluations.result: The broad objective effect persists, while local RBF CKA reverses supervised versus image-text and ImageNet-21k versus ImageNet-1k ordering relative to global linear CKA

evaluations.result: Linear CKA stabilizes around 10,000 images; RBF CKA at sigma 0.2 requires 30,000 and remains more variable

limitations: Author-stated: model attributes are correlated in the zoo, particularly objective with training-data scale, and the analysis cannot fully disentangle them.
Author-stated: SSL, supervised, and image-text representations come from systematically different layer conventions, which may contribute to objective-group differences.
Author-stated: SSL objectives are heterogeneous and that heterogeneity itself could explain their higher consistency.
Author-stated: the structured-dataset collection is small, limiting category-level conclusions about representation-behavior coupling.
Author-stated: natural single-domain versus multi-domain categories overlap and do not quantify contextual information or the continuum of domain diversity.
Reviewer-identified: the main evidence is observational and does not justify the causal verb drives without controlled retraining varying only objective.
Reviewer-identified: checkpoint lineages, model pairs, and dataset pairs are statistically dependent, but no hierarchical or block-resampled uncertainty is reported.
Reviewer-identified: densely sampled model families receive quadratically more influence than sparsely represented independent training lineages.
Reviewer-identified: objective groups contain 14, 20, and 30 checkpoints, producing unequal dyad counts and correlation precision.

Reviewer-identified: no inferential interval, dependency-preserving permutation test, effect size with uncertainty, or multiplicity adjustment supports claims that one factor matters more than another.
Reviewer-identified: the six-anchor comparison controls only broad architecture and parameter scale, not data, exact model family, optimizer, augmentation, duration, or representation stage.
Reviewer-identified: the appendix's controlled ImageNet-versus-Places result shows a strong training-domain effect that the main data-size analysis obscures.
Reviewer-identified: Pearson consistency ignores absolute CKA shifts and is sensitive to linear outliers; it is not direct transport of similarity magnitude.
Reviewer-identified: CKA and RSA are related kernel-geometry statistics, so their agreement is not independent validation of a shared-world construct.
Reviewer-identified: standard CKA/RSA can be confounded by input population structure, but no deconfounded representation-similarity baseline is included.
Reviewer-identified: final-layer geometric similarity does not establish identical decodable information, causal features, task strategy, or representation content.
Reviewer-identified: all images are center-cropped to 224 pixels rather than evaluated under every checkpoint's native resolution and inference recipe.
Reviewer-identified: model selection excludes specialized and synthetic pretraining and is restricted to public vision checkpoints available at one time.
Reviewer-identified: the ImageNet sampling result is extrapolated to datasets with very different class balance, size, and visual structure.
Reviewer-identified: performance-gap correlations have no held-out predictive evaluation and can be driven by task difficulty, ceiling effects, class structure, or correlated checkpoint families.
Reviewer-identified: the artifact's documented main configuration uses RBF sigma 0.4 on 10k subsets, not the paper's chosen sigma 0.2 on 30k subsets.
Reviewer-identified: dependencies are only partially pinned, expensive stages assume SLURM, and notebook outputs lack an automated end-to-end regression test.
failure_modes: A new checkpoint from an underrepresented objective or training domain can fall outside the zoo-derived ordering and invalidate a category median.
Adding several near-duplicate checkpoints from one family can shift a dyadic distribution without adding comparable independent evidence.
A high Pearson consistency can conceal a large shift or rescaling in every absolute model-pair CKA value.
A few extreme dyads can dominate a small group correlation, particularly when model-set sizes differ.
An extraction-layer convention can make one objective appear stable because it samples an earlier or more pooled stage of computation.
Shared resizing and center cropping can induce common geometry or suppress a model's native high-resolution features.
Input population structure can produce high conventional CKA/RSA even for representations whose functional content is not aligned.
Global linear CKA can appear stable while the local neighborhoods needed for fine-grained recognition change across datasets.
Local RBF conclusions can change with bandwidth and require substantially more stimuli than the documented reproduction subset supplies.
A model pair can be representationally close but functionally different, or functionally close through different internal strategies.
Dataset categories can proxy unmeasured class count, resolution, background context, domain shift, or label granularity rather than a single-domain construct.
Correlations between similarity and performance gap can reverse after conditioning on accuracy level, family, or task difficulty.
Training-domain restriction can yield high consistency by narrowing the solution space, which should not be mistaken for convergence toward a universal representation.
Notebook state, external intermediate files, or a config mismatch can reproduce a plausible figure using a metric different from the one described in the paper.
reusable_insights: Always report both absolute representational similarity and cross-stimulus ordering consistency; they answer different questions.
Represent the model zoo as a dependency graph of checkpoints, training runs, families, objectives, data, and extraction stages before performing pairwise inference.
Use one weight per independent training lineage or a crossed random-effects/dyadic model instead of treating every pair as independent evidence.
Bootstrap models by family and datasets as blocks, preserving the shared-node structure of pairwise correlations.
Replace title-level causal language with association unless the same architecture, data, optimization, and extraction layer are retrained under randomized objective changes.
Factorially cross objective and training domain; Appendix I shows that coarse data-size labels can hide a large domain effect.
Pre-register the representation extraction point and repeat at homologous depths to separate layer choice from objective.
Audit multiple similarity measures for invariance, sampling bias, locality, deconfounding, decodable information, and functional sensitivity rather than counting metric agreement alone.
Choose RBF bandwidth by a held-out, dimension-aware rule and pair it with a sample-size contract for every dataset.
Turn a similarity-consistency claim into a prospective task: predict held-out dataset/model similarities before adding them to the atlas.
Validate behavioral relevance with cross-decoding, causal interventions, error consistency, and held-out model selection, not only performance-gap correlation.
Quantify dataset properties such as domain diversity, background context, resolution, label granularity, and input-population structure instead of relying only on manual categories.
A narrow training domain may increase consistency by restricting admissible solutions; distinguish this from convergence toward a general world model.
Encode every paper figure's metric, bandwidth, subset size, checkpoint list, and input artifact in one machine-readable manifest tested by the reproduction pipeline.
open_questions: Does the SSL consistency advantage survive a factorial experiment with identical architecture, data, augmentations, optimizer, budget, seeds, and representation depth?
How large is the objective effect after model-family and dataset block bootstrapping or a crossed hierarchical dyadic model?
Does family-balanced subsampling preserve the reported objective ordering?
Which layer depths maximize cross-dataset consistency for each objective, and do homologous-depth comparisons remove the extraction-layer confound?
Do deconfounded CKA, task-relevant similarity, neighborhood overlap, Procrustes, and cross-decoding produce the same group conclusions?
Can the statistic prospectively predict model similarities on a held-out dataset and provide calibrated error bars?
Can one dataset's model-pair similarities improve model selection or ensemble design on another beyond metadata and ImageNet accuracy baselines?
What dataset features quantitatively explain low-consistency outliers: domain distance, class count, background context, resolution, label granularity, or intrinsic dimension?
Does native-resolution, native-crop evaluation change the results for high-resolution ViTs and image-text models?
How do specialized, synthetic-data, multimodal, generative, video, and language model families alter the observed consistency distribution?
Does high representation consistency imply transferable decoders or causal features, or can it coexist with different mechanisms and errors?
Why do Places365-supervised checkpoints exhibit greater consistency than ImageNet-supervised checkpoints, and does this replicate across additional domains and training seeds?
How should a convergence measure separate general world-model alignment from convergence caused by a restricted task or training domain?
Can an automated artifact test reconstruct every primary and appendix plot from raw public inputs with the exact stated metric configuration?

competitive_landscape.title: Position: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: the central convergence hypothesis challenged and refined by the reviewed paper
competitive_landscape.difference: Huh et al. synthesize and demonstrate representational convergence across model scale and modalities and propose a shared statistical model of reality. Ciernik et al. make the evaluation stimulus explicit and show that relative vision-model alignment depends on objective and dataset; however, their final-layer observational statistic does not directly test whether models encode the same underlying content.

competitive_landscape.title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited
competitive_landscape.relationship: foundational CKA method and representation-comparison baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Kornblith et al. motivate CKA, characterize its invariances, and show it can align layers across random initializations. The reviewed work builds a second-order correlation over CKA dyads across datasets, adding stimulus consistency but inheriting the need to justify what CKA's geometry means functionally.

competitive_landscape.title: Grounding Representation Similarity with Statistical Testing
competitive_landscape.relationship: functional sensitivity and specificity audit for representation metrics
competitive_landscape.difference: Ding et al. evaluate CKA and alternatives by whether they respond to changes that alter functional behavior and ignore changes that do not, finding disagreements and shared failures. Ciernik et al. compare metric trends and linear-probe gaps but do not apply these sensitivity/specificity tests to their cross-dataset consistency statistic.

competitive_landscape.title: Deconfounded Representation Similarity for Comparison of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct input-population confound and missing metric baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Cui et al. show that input population structure can spuriously increase RSA and CKA even for random networks and propose covariate-adjusted deconfounded similarity that better tracks OOD accuracy. Because Ciernik et al. deliberately vary the input dataset, repeating the atlas with deconfounded CKA is a decisive missing baseline for separating stimulus geometry from model geometry.

competitive_landscape.title: Wild Comparisons: A Study of How Representation Similarity Changes When Input Data Is Drawn from a Shifted Distribution
competitive_landscape.relationship: closest contemporaneous precursor on stimulus-distribution sensitivity
competitive_landscape.difference: Brown et al. directly vary in-distribution, shifted, and subpopulation inputs and report that absolute similarity changes while relative comparisons remain fairly robust in a smaller setting. Ciernik et al. scale this question to 64 models and 23 datasets and attribute heterogeneity to model/dataset groups, but do not inherit a formal distribution-shift scalar or uncertainty model.

competitive_landscape.title: Getting aligned on representational alignment
competitive_landscape.relationship: cross-disciplinary taxonomy of alignment measurements and behavior
competitive_landscape.difference: Sucholutsky et al. distinguish measurement, mutual information, bridging, and causality across machine learning and neuroscience and foreground when alignment should imply behavior. Ciernik et al. instantiate one geometric, stimulus-conditioned cell of this taxonomy; the broader framework highlights that consistency alone is not causal or semantic alignment.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivalence between representational similarity analysis, centered kernel alignment, and canonical correlations analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: mathematical dependence among purported robustness metrics
competitive_landscape.difference: Williams shows that mean-centered RSA and CKA are largely equivalent and connects them to CCA. This makes Ciernik et al.'s similar conclusions under linear CKA and RSA useful implementation robustness but weaker evidence of construct robustness than agreement among unrelated measures would be.

competitive_landscape.title: What Representational Similarity Measures Imply about Decodable Information
competitive_landscape.relationship: theoretical interpretation of similarity through linear decoding
competitive_landscape.difference: Harvey et al. derive how CKA, CCA, and other measures correspond to average alignment of optimal linear readouts. Their results provide a more precise interpretation for Ciernik et al.'s geometry, while also showing that a single CKA coefficient does not identify which tasks or features are shared.

competitive_landscape.title: Not all solutions are created equal: An analytical dissociation of functional and representational similarity in deep linear neural networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: analytical counterexample to inferring function from representation alignment
competitive_landscape.difference: Braun et al. prove and simulate that representational and functional similarity can dissociate in both directions and that generalization error need not constrain representation. This directly limits interpretation of Ciernik et al.'s performance-gap correlations and motivates functional or causal tests beyond geometry.

competitive_landscape.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
competitive_landscape.relationship: large-scale factor analysis emphasizing training-data effects
competitive_landscape.difference: Conwell et al. analyze many vision networks and report that training data is a key driver of high-level representational geometry, potentially beyond architecture, objective, or metric. Ciernik et al. cite this challenge and reproduce a strong training-domain effect only in Appendix I, which qualifies their main coarse claim that data size is less important than objective.

competitive_landscape.title: Similarity of Neural Network Models: A Survey of Functional and Representational Measures
competitive_landscape.relationship: current comprehensive map of metric properties and failure modes
competitive_landscape.difference: Klabunde et al. organize functional and representational measures, their invariances, robustness issues, and application tradeoffs. The reviewed paper supplies a new stimulus-consistency application but evaluates a narrow subset of this design space and omits several functional and deconfounded controls highlighted by the survey.

competitive_landscape.title: Causes and Consequences of Representational Similarity in Machine Learning Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct current controlled study of causes and downstream consequences
competitive_landscape.difference: This ICLR 2026-era work varies task and dataset overlap across models and modalities and evaluates consequences of the resulting alignment, moving from observational zoo stratification toward controlled causes. It is a close successor and a stronger template for testing whether objective or shared data actually creates consistency.

competitive_landscape.title: Position: An Empirically Grounded Identifiability Theory Will Accelerate Self-Supervised Learning Research
competitive_landscape.relationship: current theoretical account of SSL convergence and non-identifiability
competitive_landscape.difference: Reizinger et al. argue that finite samples, data diversity, augmentations, architecture, initialization, optimization, and dynamics all condition whether SSL representations are identifiable or converge. These are precisely the uncontrolled variables inside Ciernik et al.'s heterogeneous SSL group, so high group consistency is evidence to explain rather than an isolated objective effect.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimating Neural Representation Alignment from Sparsely Sampled Inputs and Features
competitive_landscape.difference: Chun et al. analyze CKA bias from sampling both inputs and representation features and introduce a corrected estimator. Ciernik et al. use unbiased CKA and bootstrap input subsets, a strong start, but do not test feature-sampling or dimension-dependent correction across checkpoints with radically different widths.

competitive_landscape.title: Convergence Without Understanding: When Language Models Agree on Representations but Disagree on Reasoning
competitive_landscape.relationship: current empirical dissociation between alignment, correctness, and causal reasoning
competitive_landscape.difference: Usama and Chang report high cross-model CKA even on collectively failed problems, sharp alignment changes across generation stages, and weak causal influence of shared decodable information. Although their domain is language reasoning, the results directly caution against interpreting Ciernik et al.'s stable final-layer vision geometry as shared understanding without causal tests.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-Task Pretraining Drives Representational Convergence
competitive_landscape.relationship: current controlled mechanism for objective/task-diversity-driven convergence
competitive_landscape.difference: Park uses small transformers on controlled geometric tasks and finds increasing task diversity drives CKA convergence and dominant world-map structure. This provides a causal, factorial test of one Platonic mechanism, whereas Ciernik et al.'s heterogeneous pretrained zoo cannot distinguish task diversity from data, architecture, family, or optimization.

competitive_landscape.title: Reliability of CKA as a Similarity Measure in Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct reliability audit of the primary metric
competitive_landscape.difference: This work studies when CKA behaves reliably across layer widths, architectures, initializations, and sample regimes and documents important sensitivity conditions. Ciernik et al. address stimulus count carefully on ImageNet, but a broader CKA reliability panel across model widths and representation dimensions remains a relevant missing diagnostic.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim a principled, systematic framework for measuring whether relative pairwise representational similarities transfer across datasets and for identifying model and dataset variables associated with that consistency at unprecedented vision-model scale.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper evaluates 64 public vision checkpoints on 23 datasets, correlates model-pair similarity vectors across all dataset pairs, and layers objective, architecture, data, size, metric, sampling, dataset-category, behavior, anchor, and training-domain analyses. Brown et al. had already studied how shifted or subpopulation stimuli change representation similarity, and CKA/RSA foundations and confounds were established, but the breadth of the cross-dataset model-zoo atlas and its explicit consistency distributions are a substantive empirical extension.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The descriptive framework and scale are genuinely useful and moderately novel; the strongest novel result is the separation between image-text models' high absolute similarity and SSL models' high cross-stimulus consistency. The claim that objective drives the effect is not causally novel because objective is entangled with data, family, algorithm, and extraction layer, while Appendix I shows training domain matters strongly. A defensible claim is that objective label is the most visibly associated metadata axis in this selected zoo under global linear CKA. The most important missing baselines are deconfounded CKA, dependency-aware hierarchical uncertainty, family-balanced sampling, homologous-layer analysis, and factorial same-data retraining.

reviewer_notes: Read all 29 cached pages, including appendices, tables, sampling analyses, local/global metric comparisons, anchor study, training-domain extension, and all-dataset behavioral plots. Inspected the public artifact at commit 99d8051f9985f86d1bc64fd43243d30b408c2606: core code confirms unbiased CKA by default, symmetric unique model-pair matrices, and upper-triangle extraction before Pearson correlation. The README/config path mismatch for local RBF CKA was checked directly. Competitor records were rechecked against arXiv, OpenReview, PMLR, ACM, and Nature primary pages through 2026-08-23. The review distinguishes stable relative ordering from absolute CKA transfer and descriptive association from causal factor identification.
